source.text: καὶ βαστάζων αὑτῷ τὸν σταυρὸν ἐξῆλθεν εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον Κρανίου Τόπον, ὃ λέγεται Ἑβραϊστὶ Γολγοθα, ὅπου αὐτὸν ἐσταύρωσαν, καὶ μετ’ αὐτοῦ ἄλλους δύο ἐντεῦθεν καὶ ἐντεῦθεν, μέσον δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν.

records.literal_gloss: And carrying for himself the cross he went out to the [place] being called Of-a-Skull Place, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha, \v 18 where him they crucified, and with him others two, on this side and on that side, and in the middle the Jesus.

en.L: And carrying the cross by {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went out to the [place] called Place of a Skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha, \v 18 where they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} two others, on this side and on that side, and Jesus in the middle.
en.B: Carrying the cross by {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went out to what is called the Place of the Skull (in Hebrew, Golgotha). \v 18 There they crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, along with two others, one on each side and Jesus in the middle.
en.R: Jesus carried {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own cross and went out of the city to a place called Skull Place. In the Hebrew language its name is Golgotha. \v 18 There the soldiers nailed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to the cross. They also crucified two other men, one on each side of Jesus, so that Jesus was in the middle.

decisions.choice: carrying the cross by himself, with no one's help
alternatives: carrying the cross for his own sake
only that he set out carrying it, leaving open whether someone helped later
decisions.reason: The small word attached to "carrying" points back to Jesus: the cross was his own load. Matthew, Mark and Luke say the soldiers made Simon of Cyrene carry it (Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26). John does not mention Simon. The accounts can be read together (Jesus set out carrying it and Simon took it over on the way), but John's own telling shows Jesus carrying it himself.

decisions.choice: the cross: probably the crossbeam, which a condemned man carried to the place of execution
alternatives: the whole cross, upright and crossbeam
decisions.reason: Roman practice was for the condemned person to carry his cross to the place of execution, where the upright post often stood ready. What he carried was most likely the crossbeam, since a whole cross would have been too heavy for one man, especially one who had been flogged (19:1). John only says "the cross".

decisions.choice: Place of a Skull, in the local language Golgotha: John translates the name for his readers
decisions.reason: John gives the meaning of the name before the local name itself. "Hebrew" is John's word for the language of the Jews of the land, which in daily speech was mostly Aramaic, and Golgotha is the Aramaic word for "skull" (see 5:2; 19:13). Why it had that name is not known; it may have been the shape of the ground. The place was outside the city but near it (19:20; Hebrews 13:12).

decisions.choice: they crucified him: the Roman soldiers, as 19:23 says; and two others, whom John does not name
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject, and 19:16 says Pilate handed Jesus over "to them". But 19:23 says plainly that the soldiers crucified Jesus: crucifixion was a Roman penalty, carried out by Roman soldiers on the governor's order. John does not say who the other two men were; the other Gospels call them bandits or criminals (Mark 15:27; Luke 23:32-33).

decisions.choice: the soldiers nailed him to the cross (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the soldiers, from 19:23 (meaning decision m4), so that young readers do not take "they" to mean the last group mentioned. "Nailed" comes from the nail marks in 20:25 and explains the word "crucified" for readers who may not know it.

decisions.choice: Place of a Skull (L); the Place of the Skull (B); Skull Place (R); in Hebrew (every level)
decisions.reason: Each level gives John's own translation of the name. "Calvary" comes from the Latin word for skull and is not in the Greek. "Hebrew" keeps the word John used; meaning decision m3 explains which language this was.

source.text: ἔγραψεν δὲ καὶ τίτλον ὁ Πιλᾶτος καὶ ἔθηκεν ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ· ἦν δὲ γεγραμμένον· Ἰησοῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων.

records.literal_gloss: Wrote and also a title the Pilate and put [it] on the cross; was and written: Jesus the Nazorean the king of the Jews.

en.L: And Pilate also wrote a notice and put [it] on the cross; and it was written: "Jesus the Nazorean, the King of the Jews."
en.B: Pilate also wrote a notice and had it placed on the cross. The wording was: "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews."
en.R: Pilate also wrote a sign and had it put on the cross. It said, "Jesus from Nazareth, the King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: a notice: a placard stating the charge, the Latin titulus
alternatives: an inscription carved on the cross
decisions.reason: The Greek word is the Latin "titulus", a board or placard with writing on it. Roman writers mention a placard naming a condemned person's crime, carried before him or hung on him; here it is fixed to the cross. The charge is the one Jesus was tried for: claiming to be a king (18:33-37; 19:12).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish nation, in the title of a king
decisions.reason: In "King of the Jews" the word names the people as a nation, as in Pilate's questions (18:33, 39) and the soldiers' mockery (19:3). It is the Roman charge against Jesus, in Pilate's words, and it is kept as written at every level.

decisions.choice: the charge is also true in John's telling: Jesus is the King of Israel
decisions.reason: Pilate meant the notice as the charge, perhaps with scorn for the people (19:15). John has already shown that Jesus is king in a sense Pilate did not grasp (1:49; 12:13-15; 18:36-37), so the notice says more than its writer intended, as Caiaphas's words did (11:50-52).

decisions.choice: Pilate wrote and put: he is responsible for the notice, whether or not his own hand did the work
alternatives: Pilate wrote it with his own hand
decisions.reason: A governor would normally have such a notice made and put up by others, and Greek often says that a person did what he had done. What matters to the story is that the wording is Pilate's, as he insists in 19:22.

decisions.choice: notice (L, B); sign (R); the Nazorean (L); of Nazareth (B); from Nazareth (R)
decisions.reason: "Title" now usually means the name of a book or a rank, so "notice" and "sign" say what the board was. Literal keeps the form of the word for Jesus's home town, which John uses (18:5, 7); Balanced and Readable say what it means.

source.text: τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τίτλον πολλοὶ ἀνέγνωσαν τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὅτι ἐγγὺς ἦν ὁ τόπος τῆς πόλεως ὅπου ἐσταυρώθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς· καὶ ἦν γεγραμμένον Ἑβραϊστί, Ῥωμαϊστί, Ἑλληνιστί.

records.literal_gloss: This then the title many read of the Jews, because near was the place of the city where was crucified the Jesus; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, in Greek.

en.L: So many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, in Greek.
en.B: Many of the Jews of Jerusalem read this notice, since the spot where Jesus was crucified was close to the city. The notice was in Hebrew, Latin and Greek.
en.R: Many Jewish people from Jerusalem read the sign, because the place where Jesus hung on the cross was close to the city. The sign was written in three languages: Hebrew, Latin and Greek.

decisions.choice: the Jews: people of Jerusalem and the festival crowds who passed by
decisions.reason: Here the word means ordinary people who saw the notice because the place was near the city, at Passover when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims. The authorities appear separately in the next sentence as "the chief priests of the Jews".

decisions.choice: near the city: outside the walls, where many people would pass
decisions.reason: Executions took place outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35-36; Hebrews 13:12). The Romans crucified people where many would see them, as a warning, and John notes it to explain why so many read the notice.

decisions.choice: Hebrew, Latin, Greek: the local language, the language of Rome, and the common language of the eastern empire
decisions.reason: "Hebrew" is John's word for the language of the Jews of the land, mostly Aramaic in daily speech (19:17). The second word is literally "in Roman", meaning Latin, the language of the Roman government. Greek was spoken across the eastern Mediterranean. In all three languages the notice could be read by everyone in the city at the festival.

decisions.choice: Hebrew, Latin, Greek (SBLGNT)
alternatives: Hebrew, Greek, Latin (many later manuscripts; the King James Version follows this order)
decisions.reason: The manuscripts list the three languages in different orders. The order Hebrew, Latin, Greek is found in several early manuscripts; many later ones read Hebrew, Greek, Latin. The meaning is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jews of Jerusalem (B); Jewish people from Jerusalem (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people who were there (meaning decision m1), as in 8:48 and 10:31. "Jerusalem" is the city of this sentence ("near the city").

source.text: ἔλεγον οὖν τῷ Πιλάτῳ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς τῶν Ἰουδαίων· Μὴ γράφε· Ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ἀλλ’ ὅτι ἐκεῖνος εἶπεν Βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων εἰμί.

records.literal_gloss: Were saying then to the Pilate the chief priests of the Jews: Not write: The king of the Jews, but that that one said: King of the Jews I am.

en.L: So the chief priests of the Jews were saying to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but that that man said, 'I am King of the Jews.'"
en.B: The chief priests of the Jews objected. "Do not write 'The King of the Jews,'" they told Pilate. "Write that this man said, 'I am King of the Jews.'"
en.R: So the chief priests of the Jews kept telling Pilate, "Do not write 'The King of the Jews.' Write that this man claimed to be King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: the chief priests of the Jews: the leading priests in Jerusalem, as heads of the nation
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Only here does John call them "the chief priests of the Jews". The phrase sets their title beside the one on the cross: the nation's chief priests object to the nation's king. It names the group that objected, the leading priests (18:35; 19:6, 15), not the people.

decisions.choice: were saying ... do not write: an objection pressed more than once, asking Pilate to change what he had put up
alternatives: a request made before the notice was written
decisions.reason: The verb of saying is in a tense that can describe a continuing or repeated action. The command "do not write" is in the present tense: Pilate had already written it (19:19), so they want the wording changed.

decisions.choice: that man said, 'I am King of the Jews': they want the title shown as his claim, not as fact
decisions.reason: The word for "that man" keeps Jesus at a distance, with contempt. As written, the notice states that he is the king; with their change it would only report his claim.

decisions.choice: objected ... they told Pilate (B); kept telling (R); Write that this man ... (B); claimed to be (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the continuing objection with a verb English uses for it (meaning decision m2), and break the request into two sentences. Readable reports the claim indirectly to avoid quotation marks inside quotation marks.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Ὃ γέγραφα γέγραφα.

records.literal_gloss: Answered the Pilate: What I have written, I have written.

en.L: Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
en.B: Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
en.R: Pilate answered, "What I have written will stay as I wrote it."

decisions.choice: What I have written, I have written: it stands and will not be changed
decisions.reason: Greek uses this tense for an action that is done and whose result remains. Saying it twice makes the answer final.

decisions.choice: Pilate's refusal: the governor will not let the priests change his notice
alternatives: Pilate refuses because he believes Jesus is a king
decisions.reason: John does not give Pilate's reason. The priests had just forced his hand (19:12-16), and the notice is a way of answering them. Pilate, who gave way on the sentence, does not give way on the wording, so the title stands over the cross.

decisions.choice: What I have written will stay as I wrote it (R)
alternatives: What I have written, I have written
decisions.reason: Readers new to the Bible may not hear a refusal in the repeated phrase, so Readable says what it means (meaning decision m1).

source.text: οἱ οὖν στρατιῶται ὅτε ἐσταύρωσαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἔλαβον τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐποίησαν τέσσαρα μέρη, ἑκάστῳ στρατιώτῃ μέρος, καὶ τὸν χιτῶνα.

records.literal_gloss: The then soldiers, when they crucified the Jesus, took the garments of him and made four parts, to each soldier a part, and the tunic.

en.L: Then the soldiers, when they crucified Jesus, took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and [took] the tunic.
en.B: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes and divided them into four shares, one share for each soldier. They also took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} tunic.
en.R: After the soldiers had nailed Jesus to the cross, they took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes and split them into four parts, one part for each soldier. They also took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} tunic, the long shirt {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wore next to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} skin.

decisions.choice: four soldiers: a Roman squad of four carried out the crucifixion
decisions.reason: Roman soldiers often worked in groups of four (compare Acts 12:4). The clothes of a person being executed were usually taken by those who carried out the sentence. The sentence names the Roman soldiers plainly as the ones who crucified Jesus.

decisions.choice: garments: his outer clothing (cloak, belt, sandals and the like); tunic: the long shirt worn next to the skin
alternatives: garments and tunic as two words for the same clothing
decisions.reason: The plural word for garments means outer clothes in general. The tunic was the inner garment, a long shirt reaching to the knees or ankles, worn under the cloak. John sets the tunic apart because of what happens to it next.

decisions.choice: garments (L); clothes (B, R); tunic at every level, explained at Readable
decisions.reason: "Tunic" is the exact word for the long inner shirt; "coat" or "robe" would suggest an outer garment. Readable adds a short description for young readers.

source.text: ἦν δὲ ὁ χιτὼν ἄραφος, ἐκ τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑφαντὸς δι’ ὅλου·

records.literal_gloss: Was now the tunic seamless, from the top woven through whole.

en.L: Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top through the whole.
en.B: The tunic was seamless, woven in a single piece from top to bottom.
en.R: This tunic had no seams. It was woven in one piece, from the top all the way down.

decisions.choice: from the top: woven from the top down, in one piece
decisions.reason: John uses the same word elsewhere for "from above" (3:31; 19:11), and "again, from above" (3:3, 7). Here it describes the weaving, from the neck down, with no seam.

decisions.choice: the detail explains why the soldiers did not tear it; John may also see more in it
alternatives: a sign that Jesus is high priest, whose robe was woven without a seam
a picture of the unity of Jesus's people, who are not to be torn apart
decisions.reason: The plain reason for the detail is the next sentence: a seamless tunic was worth more whole. Two further meanings have been proposed. The high priest's robe was to be woven so that it would not tear (Exodus 28:32), and the Jewish historian Josephus says it was not made of two pieces but woven in one. And the word "tear" (19:24) is the word John uses for divisions among people (7:43; 9:16; 10:19) and for the net that was not torn (21:11). John does not say that he means either, so this is uncertain.

decisions.choice: in a single piece from top to bottom (B); in one piece, from the top all the way down (R)
decisions.reason: "Through the whole" means it was woven all in one; Balanced and Readable say so plainly.

source.text: εἶπαν οὖν πρὸς ἀλλήλους· Μὴ σχίσωμεν αὐτόν, ἀλλὰ λάχωμεν περὶ αὐτοῦ τίνος ἔσται· ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ ἡ λέγουσα· Διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτιά μου ἑαυτοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου ἔβαλον κλῆρον.

records.literal_gloss: They said then to one another: Not let us tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it will be; so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, the [one] saying: They divided the garments of me among themselves, and for the clothing of me they cast a lot.

en.L: So they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, [to see] whose it will be," so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says, "They divided {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} garments among themselves, and for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} clothing they cast a lot."
en.B: So they said to each other, "Let us not tear it. Let us cast lots for it and see who gets it." This was so that the Scripture would be fulfilled that says, "They shared out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} garments among themselves, and for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} clothing they cast lots."
en.R: So the soldiers said to each other, "Let us not tear it. Let us draw lots to see who will get it." This happened to make the Scripture come true that says, "They divided {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} clothes among themselves, and they drew lots for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} clothing."

decisions.choice: cast lots: a game of chance to decide who would have it
decisions.reason: Lots were marked stones or pieces of bone, thrown or drawn to decide a matter. Soldiers also played with dice. Either way, chance decided which soldier kept the tunic whole.

decisions.choice: Psalm 22:19, quoted word for word from the Greek translation of the psalm
decisions.reason: The words are those of Psalm 22:19 (22:18 in Bibles that do not count the title as a verse) in the Greek translation used in John's day, which follows the Hebrew closely. The psalm is the prayer of a righteous sufferer, surrounded by enemies, who is rescued by God; its first line is Jesus's cry in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34. John uses it to show that what the soldiers did was foretold.

decisions.choice: John reads the psalm's two lines as two acts: the garments divided, the tunic given by lot
alternatives: the two lines say one thing twice, as Hebrew poetry often does
decisions.reason: In the psalm the two lines are parallel and describe one act. John's account matches each line to a separate deed: the soldiers divide the outer garments (19:23) and cast lots for the tunic.

decisions.choice: so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: the narrator's comment on God's purpose, not the soldiers' aim
alternatives: the soldiers acted in order to fulfill Scripture
decisions.reason: The soldiers knew nothing of the psalm. John's formula (12:38; 13:18; 15:25; 19:36) says that what happened was in keeping with what God had said beforehand.

decisions.choice: This was so that ... (B); This happened to make ... come true (R)
alternatives: so that the Scripture might be fulfilled (Literal, joined to the soldiers' words)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable start a new sentence for John's comment so that it is not read as part of what the soldiers said (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: draw lots (R); cast lots (L, B)
decisions.reason: "Draw lots" is the plainer phrase for young readers and keeps the sense of chance without naming a game the text does not name.

source.text: Οἱ μὲν οὖν στρατιῶται ταῦτα ἐποίησαν.

records.literal_gloss: The on the one hand then soldiers these things did.

en.L: So the soldiers did these things.
en.B: That is what the soldiers did.
en.R: So that is what the soldiers did.

decisions.choice: a closing line that sets the soldiers against the women in the next sentence
decisions.reason: The small word in this sentence, answered by another in the next (19:25), sets the two scenes side by side: on one side the soldiers dividing his clothes, on the other the women and the disciple standing by the cross.

decisions.choice: That is what the soldiers did (B); So that is what the soldiers did (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the sentence sound like the close of the scene, which is its job in the Greek (meaning decision m1).

source.text: Εἱστήκεισαν δὲ παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ ἀδελφὴ τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ, Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Κλωπᾶ καὶ Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή.

records.literal_gloss: Had stood now by the cross of the Jesus the mother of him and the sister of the mother of him, Mary the [one] of Clopas, and Mary the Magdalene.

en.L: But standing by the cross of Jesus were {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother's sister, Mary the [wife] of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
en.B: Meanwhile, near the cross of Jesus stood {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
en.R: Some women were standing near the cross of Jesus. They were {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

decisions.choice: four women: his mother, his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
alternatives: three women: his mother's sister is Mary the wife of Clopas
two women: his mother and her sister, named as the two Marys
decisions.reason: The Greek has no "and" between "his mother's sister" and "Mary of Clopas", so they could be the same woman. But then two sisters would both be called Mary, which is unlikely. Read as four, the list falls into two pairs joined by "and": two women not named, then two named Marys. The evidence is not decisive.

decisions.choice: Mary the wife of Clopas
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "Mary of Clopas", a way of naming a woman by a man she belonged to, most often her husband, sometimes her father or son. "Wife" is the usual sense. Nothing more is known of Clopas; whether he is the Cleopas of Luke 24:18 is uncertain.

decisions.choice: Magdalene: from Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee
decisions.reason: Mary Magdalene is named here for the first time in John; she is the first to find the tomb empty and to see the risen Jesus (20:1-18). Luke 8:2 says Jesus had freed her from seven demons.

decisions.choice: his mother's sister: John does not name her
decisions.reason: Other Gospels name women at the cross: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome or the mother of Zebedee's sons (Matthew 27:56; Mark 15:40). Whether John's unnamed sister of Jesus's mother is one of these cannot be known from the text.

decisions.choice: Meanwhile (B); Some women were standing (R)
decisions.reason: The sentence turns from the soldiers to the people who loved Jesus (19:24 meaning decision m1). Balanced marks the turn with "Meanwhile"; Readable starts with the women and then lists them, without saying how many (meaning decision m1).

source.text: Ἰησοῦς οὖν ἰδὼν τὴν μητέρα καὶ τὸν μαθητὴν παρεστῶτα ὃν ἠγάπα λέγει τῇ μητρί· Γύναι, ἴδε ὁ υἱός σου·

records.literal_gloss: Jesus then, having seen the mother and the disciple standing by whom he loved, says to the mother: Woman, behold the son of you.

en.L: So Jesus, seeing {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother and the disciple whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} loved standing by, says to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother, "Woman, look, your son."
en.B: Jesus saw {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother there, and near her the disciple whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} loved. He said to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother, "Woman, look, here is your son."
en.R: Jesus saw {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother there. The disciple whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} loved was standing near her. Jesus said to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mother, "Mother, he is your son now."

decisions.choice: Woman: a respectful address, as at Cana
decisions.reason: Jesus uses this address to his mother only twice, at Cana (2:4) and here. At Cana he said, "My hour has not yet come"; now his hour has come (12:23; 13:1; 17:1), and at the cross he speaks to her again in the same way. The address was courteous, not rude.

decisions.choice: look, your son: a declaration that makes a new bond, the disciple to be her son
alternatives: only pointing out the disciple standing there
decisions.reason: The words do not simply point at someone; they give the disciple to her as a son, and the next sentence gives her to him as a mother. The disciple acts on it at once (19:27).

decisions.choice: a dying son's care for his mother; perhaps also the start of a new family of his disciples
alternatives: chiefly a symbol, with the mother standing for a people of faith
decisions.reason: The first sense is plain: Jesus makes sure his mother will be cared for. His brothers did not yet believe in him (7:5). John may also mean more: from the cross Jesus joins his mother and his disciple as one family, and after the resurrection he calls his disciples "my brothers" (20:17). The text does not say so directly.

decisions.choice: the disciple whom Jesus loved: the disciple John does not name
decisions.reason: This disciple first appears at the last supper (13:23) and stands at the cross when the other disciples have scattered (16:32). The Gospel says he is the source of its witness (19:35; 21:24).

decisions.choice: said (B, R); says (L), and so through this passage (19:27, 19:28)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English normally tells a story. This applies to every such verb in this passage.

decisions.choice: Woman
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "Woman" so that readers can connect this scene with Cana (2:4); the footnote on meaning decision m1 says the address was respectful. "Dear woman" would add warmth the word does not carry on its own.

decisions.choice: Mother, he is your son now (R)
decisions.reason: For young readers "Woman" sounds rude, which the Greek is not. She is his mother, so Readable uses the address a son would use, as it does at 2:4. "Now" shows that the words make a new bond (meaning decision m2).

source.text: εἶτα λέγει τῷ μαθητῇ· Ἴδε ἡ μήτηρ σου.

records.literal_gloss: Then he says to the disciple: Behold the mother of you.

en.L: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to the disciple, "Look, your mother."
en.B: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to the disciple, "Look, here is your mother."
en.R: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to the disciple, "She is your mother now."

decisions.choice: look, your mother: the other half of the declaration in 19:26
decisions.reason: The two sayings match: she is to be his mother, and he is to be her son. Together they put her in the disciple's care as a son cares for his mother.

decisions.choice: She is your mother now (R)
decisions.reason: As in 19:26, Readable says what the words do, giving the disciple a mother to care for.

source.text: καὶ ἀπ’ ἐκείνης τῆς ὥρας ἔλαβεν ὁ μαθητὴς αὐτὴν εἰς τὰ ἴδια.

records.literal_gloss: And from that the hour took the disciple her into the own [things].

en.L: And from that hour the disciple took her into his own [home].
en.B: From that time on the disciple took her into his own home.
en.R: From then on, that disciple took her to live in his home.

decisions.choice: from that hour: from that time on, starting then
alternatives: from Jesus's appointed hour, meaning the cross as the hour of his glory
decisions.reason: Here "hour" means a time of day: the disciple acted at once. But John has spoken of Jesus's hour throughout the Gospel (2:4; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1), and at the cross that hour has come, so the word may also remind readers of it.

decisions.choice: into his own: into his own home, as one of his household
alternatives: into his own care, without saying where she lived
decisions.reason: "His own" is a common way of saying "his home" or "his own people" (1:11; 16:32). Taking her into it means more than a place to stay: she became part of his household.

decisions.choice: From that time on (B); From then on (R); from that hour (L)
decisions.reason: Here "hour" is a time of day, not Jesus's appointed hour (which Balanced writes as "hour"), so Balanced and Readable say "time". Literal keeps "hour" so that the possible echo can be seen (meaning decision m1).

source.text: Μετὰ τοῦτο εἰδὼς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤδη πάντα τετέλεσται ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ γραφὴ λέγει· Διψῶ.

records.literal_gloss: After this, knowing the Jesus that already all things have been finished, so that might be completed the Scripture, says: I thirst.

en.L: After this, Jesus, knowing that all things had now been finished, so that the Scripture might be completed, says, "I thirst."
en.B: After this, Jesus knew that everything had now been finished. So that the Scripture would be completed, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I am thirsty."
en.R: After this, Jesus knew that everything {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had come to do was now finished. To make the Scripture come fully true, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I am thirsty."

decisions.choice: so that the Scripture might be completed goes with "he says": he said "I thirst" to fulfill the Scripture
alternatives: it goes with "all things had been finished": everything was done so that the Scripture would be completed
decisions.reason: The purpose clause stands between the two verbs and could belong to either. Joined to "he says", it explains the saying by the Scripture about thirst (meaning decision m3), as 19:24 and 19:36 explain other details. Joined to "finished", it would say that the whole work was done to complete the Scripture, and "I thirst" would be simply his need. Both readings are possible.

decisions.choice: finished ... completed: the work the Father gave Jesus is done; the Scripture is brought to completion
decisions.reason: The first verb is the one Jesus says in 19:30, "It is finished". The second is not John's usual word for fulfilling Scripture (19:24) but the word Jesus used for completing the Father's work (4:34; 5:36; 17:4). John uses it to show that the Scripture, like the work, has reached its goal.

decisions.choice: I thirst: Psalm 69:22, with Psalm 22:16 in the background
alternatives: only a statement of physical thirst, with no Scripture in mind
decisions.reason: Psalm 69:22 says "for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink" (69:21 in Bibles that do not count the title as a verse), and the next verse in John has the sour wine. Psalm 22, already quoted in 19:24, says "my tongue sticks to my jaws" (22:16; 22:15 in those Bibles). Both psalms are prayers of the righteous sufferer. The thirst was real: he had been flogged and had hung on the cross for hours.

decisions.choice: knowing: Jesus goes to his death aware and in control
decisions.reason: John often says what Jesus knew at turning points of the passion (13:1, 3; 18:4). He lays down his life of his own accord (10:18), and he speaks this word knowing that his work is now done.

decisions.choice: finished (as in 19:30); completed (as in 17:4); I thirst (L); I am thirsty (B, R)
alternatives: I am thirsty at every level
decisions.reason: "Finished" is the same English word as Jesus's last saying (19:30), and "completed" the same as "having completed the work" in 17:4, so the links in the Greek stay visible (meaning decision m2). Readable says what had been finished, from 17:4.

source.text: σκεῦος ἔκειτο ὄξους μεστόν· σπόγγον οὖν μεστὸν τοῦ ὄξους ὑσσώπῳ περιθέντες προσήνεγκαν αὐτοῦ τῷ στόματι.

records.literal_gloss: A vessel was lying of sour wine full; a sponge then full of the sour wine on hyssop having put around, they brought [it] to him the mouth.

en.L: A jar full of sour wine was standing [there]; so, putting a sponge full of the sour wine on hyssop, they brought [it] to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mouth.
en.B: A jar full of sour wine stood there. So they put a sponge soaked in the sour wine on a stalk of hyssop and raised it to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} lips.
en.R: A jar of sour wine was sitting nearby. So they soaked a sponge in it, put the sponge on the end of a hyssop stick, and lifted it up to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mouth.

decisions.choice: sour wine: cheap wine gone sour, the everyday drink of soldiers and laborers
alternatives: drugged wine offered to dull pain
decisions.reason: The word means wine that has turned sour, which mixed with water was a common drink for soldiers and workers. It is the word in the Greek of Psalm 69:22 (see 19:28). Giving it may have been simple relief rather than mockery; John does not say. It is not the wine mixed with myrrh that Mark says Jesus refused before he was crucified (Mark 15:23).

decisions.choice: hyssop: the plant used to put the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts
alternatives: only the nearest plant stem, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: Hyssop is a small, bushy plant. Israel used a bunch of it to put the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorframes (Exodus 12:22), and it was used in cleansing (Leviticus 14:4; Psalm 51:9). John has told the story so that Jesus dies on the day the Passover lambs are killed (18:28; 19:14) and calls him the Lamb of God (1:29); he applies a Passover rule to him in 19:36. The mention of hyssop most likely points to this.

decisions.choice: on hyssop (all manuscripts)
alternatives: on a javelin: a guess, found in one late manuscript, that a similar word for the Roman javelin (in Latin, pilum) stood here
decisions.reason: A stalk of hyssop seems too weak to lift a soaked sponge, so it has been suggested that John wrote a very similar word meaning "javelin", and that a copyist misread it. The guess appears in only one late manuscript, of about the eleventh century; all the early manuscripts read "hyssop". A small branch would be enough, since a cross was often not much higher than a man. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they: the people standing by the cross, most likely the soldiers
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. The soldiers are the last group said to act (19:23-24), and sour wine was their drink, so they are the most likely ones.

decisions.choice: jar; sour wine; hyssop (L); a stalk of hyssop (B); a hyssop stick (R)
decisions.reason: "Vinegar" today means something no one drinks; "sour wine" says what it was (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable say what part of the plant was used. Every level keeps "hyssop" so the Passover link can be seen (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ὅτε οὖν ἔλαβεν τὸ ὄξος ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Τετέλεσται, καὶ κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν παρέδωκεν τὸ πνεῦμα.

records.literal_gloss: When then took the sour wine the Jesus, he said: It has been finished, and having bowed the head he handed over the spirit.

en.L: So when Jesus had received the sour wine, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "It is finished," and bowing {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} handed over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit.
en.B: When Jesus had taken the sour wine, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "It is finished." Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} bowed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head and handed over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit.
en.R: Jesus drank the sour wine and said, "It is finished." Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} bowed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head, handed over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit, and died.

decisions.choice: It is finished: the work is completed, carried through to its goal, and it stands
alternatives: it is over: his life has ended
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring something to its end or goal. It is the word of 19:28, and it answers Jesus's words about completing the work the Father gave him (4:34; 17:4) and loving his own "to the end" (13:1). The tense means a thing done whose result remains. It is a cry of completion, not of defeat.

decisions.choice: handed over his spirit: he died, giving up his life himself
alternatives: breathed his last, with nothing more meant
decisions.reason: "To give up the spirit" is a way of saying someone died, and "spirit" here is his own life and breath, as in Luke 23:46. John's verb is the one used all through the passion for handing someone over (Judas, 18:2, 5; the chief priests, 18:30, 35; Pilate, 19:16). Now Jesus hands over his own life: no one takes it from him (10:18).

decisions.choice: his own spirit; John may also hint that the Spirit is now to be given
alternatives: a plain statement that he died, with no reference to the Holy Spirit
he handed over the Holy Spirit to those at the cross
decisions.reason: John said the Spirit would be given once Jesus was glorified (7:39), and the risen Jesus breathes on the disciples and gives them the Holy Spirit (20:22). Some read a hint of that here, since the words could also mean "handed over the Spirit". But the phrase is a natural way to describe death, and the Spirit is given in 20:22. The sense "his own spirit" is certain; a further hint is possible but not clear.

decisions.choice: bowing his head: first he bowed his head, then he died
decisions.reason: The order of the words shows the order of events: Jesus bows his head and then hands over his spirit, as one who chooses the moment.

decisions.choice: It is finished (every level); handed over his spirit, with "spirit" in lowercase
decisions.reason: "Finished" is the word used in 19:28, so the link stays visible. "Handed over" keeps the verb John uses throughout the passion (meaning decision m2). "Spirit" is lowercase because it is his own spirit (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: and died (R)
decisions.reason: Young readers may not know that "handed over his spirit" means that he died, so Readable says it plainly.
